food.text: In 2011, Japan overtook France to become the country with the most 3-starred Michelin restaurants. As of 2018, Tokyo held the title of the city with the most 3-starred restaurants in the world. In 2013, Japanese cuisine was added to the UNESCO Intangible Heritage List.

Traditionally, the Japanese shunned meat because of Buddhism. With the modernization of Japan in the 1880s, meat-based dishes such as tonkatsu and yakiniku became common. Foreign-inspired foods like ramen, gyōza, curry and hamburgers were adapted to Japanese tastes and ingredients.

Under Japanese rule, more Korean rice was exported to Japan, and per capita rice consumption among Koreans fell. Between 1932 and 1936 it dropped to half the level of 1912 to 1916. By 1944, per capita consumption of food grains was 35 percent below that of 1912 to 1916.
Ramen is believed to have originated in China. It became popular in Japan after the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937 to 1945), when many Chinese students were displaced to Japan.

In most of Japan, rice used to be eaten at almost every meal. A 2007 survey showed that 70% of Japanese still eat it once or twice a day, but its popularity is declining. In the 20th century, more people began choosing wheat-based products such as bread and noodles over rice.

As sugar became cheaper, chefs in the early 20th century began using it more in savory cooking, including in sushi rice. Sugar on toast became a popular breakfast because it took far less time than cooking rice. Sugar came to symbolize civilized modernity, while rural cuisines without it were seen as inferior.

By 1935, 90% of Japan's sugar was sourced from Taiwan. According to Bank of Japan estimates, by 1939 the average Japanese person ate 33 pounds (15 kg) of sugar a year. In World War II, sugar became the first food rationed on a national level.

In 1919, the sugary-milk beverage Calpis was created in Japan. Around the same time, the public ate growing amounts of sugary confections such as chocolates and caramels. Records from the 1920s show the Imperial army being fed curries and stews flavored with sugar, and doughnuts for dessert.

Okara is the pulp left over from making tofu and soy milk. In 1983 it was estimated that Japan produced about 70,000 metric tons of it a year. In Japan it is used in a side dish called unohana, cooked with soy sauce, mirin, carrots, burdock root and shiitake mushrooms.

Sunjae, born in 1956, is a Buddhist nun known as Korea's first master of temple cuisine. She left home in 1980 to join the Sinheungsa temple and focus on temple cuisine. She describes food as medicine and credits her temple diet for curing her liver cirrhosis. In 2018 she was selected to lead the Korean Food Promotion Institution and began traveling the world speaking about Korean cuisine.

art.text: Japanese contemporary art has produced many internationally significant names. Yayoi Kusama, Yoshitomo Nara, Hiroshi Sugimoto, Chiharu Shiota, Daidō Moriyama, Mariko Mori, Aya Takano and Tabaimo are all considered significant artists in the field.

Japanese art has had a large effect beyond Japan. It is valued for its simplicity and also for its colorful exuberance, and it has considerably influenced 19th-century Western painting and 20th-century Western architecture.
In 1949, Kenzō Tange won the competition to design the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum. The win gave him international acclaim, and the museum was completed in 1955.

The Japan Fine Arts Exhibition, known as Nitten, claims to be the largest combined art exhibition of its kind in the world. It has five sections: Nihonga and Western Style Painting, Sculpture, Crafts and Calligraphy.

Tange's Hiroshima success led to a series of commissions, including the Kagawa Prefectural Office Building in Takamatsu (1958) and Old Kurashiki City Hall (1960). At Kagawa, he fused elements of Heian period design with the International Style, reflecting his interest in Japanese architectural tradition.

In 1919 the Imperial Fine Arts Academy was established by imperial decree, first headed by Mori Ōgai. It absorbed the earlier Fine Arts Reviewing Committee, and the Bunten exhibition, first held in 1907, was renamed the Teiten.
In 1946, the War Damage Rehabilitation Board put forward ideas for the reconstruction of thirteen Japanese cities. Architect Kenzō Tange submitted proposals for Hiroshima and Maebashi.

After the war, Japan faced a chronic housing shortage. In 1946 the Prefabricated Housing Association was formed, and architects like Kunio Maekawa submitted designs, but government support in law for private-sector housing only came with the Public Housing Act in 1951.

The academy became the Imperial Art Academy in 1937, and its annual exhibition was renamed the Shinbunten. After World War II it became the Japan Art Academy, and the show became the Nitten from 1946, with spring and fall editions to make up for the lack of an exhibition in 1945.

Japanese homes traditionally involved sitting on cushions or on the floor. Chairs and high tables were not widely used until the 20th century, while Japan had already begun incorporating much Western, modern and post-modern architecture into its design since the 19th century.

In 2013 the Nitten awarded none of its top prizes in any of its five sections. This followed the revelation of fraudulent judging in the calligraphy section of the fiscal 2009 show, and it was the first time since 1958 that no prizes were awarded.

The Japan Art Association was a traditionalist body, and in the 1930s its painting titles began to lose their kanji characters. Its talented young painters eventually gave up on it and shifted their activity to the Bunten, a sign that Japanese painting had lost its position as the mainstream of the art world.

war.text: On 25 June 1950, North Korea's Korean People's Army invaded South Korea, starting a war that lasted until 27 July 1953. UN forces under a unified command came from 21 countries, with the US providing around 90% of military personnel. The war caused around one million military deaths and an estimated 1.5 million to 3 million civilian deaths.

After World War II ended in 1945, Korea, which had been a Japanese colony for 35 years, was divided by the Soviet Union and the United States into two occupation zones at the 38th parallel. The zones formed their own governments in 1948, led by Kim Il Sung in Pyongyang and Syngman Rhee in Seoul.

On 6 and 9 August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The two bombs killed approximately 120,000 to 140,000 people in a matter of minutes, and as many again from nuclear radiation in the following weeks, months and years. By the end of 1945 the bombs had killed as many as 140,000 people in Hiroshima and 80,000 in Nagasaki. The Soviet Union declared war and invaded Manchuria on 8 August, and these events led to the surrender of Japan on 15 August.

The Second Sino-Japanese War was fought between 1937 and 1945 and was the largest Asian war of the 20th century. It is often regarded as the beginning of World War II in Asia, because the wars became heavily intertwined after Japan attacked the United States. It killed around 20 million people, mostly Chinese civilians. Japan carried out the largest attacks in the history of biological warfare, causing at least 200,000 deaths, and used chemical weapons including lethal blister agents.

On 18 September 1931, the Japanese staged the Mukden incident, a false flag event fabricated to justify their invasion of Manchuria. Kwantung Army soldiers set off a bomb on the South Manchuria Railway to provoke an opportunity to act in "self defense". After five months of fighting, Japan occupied all of Manchuria and established the puppet state of Manchukuo. The incident is sometimes marked as the beginning of the war.

In the early hours of 7 December 1941, Japanese carrier aircraft struck the American naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, knocking eight American battleships out of action, destroying 188 aircraft and killing 2,403 Americans. Japan also attacked the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, and the British colonies of Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong. Japan declared war only after its forces had already struck, and then achieved great success over the next six months.

In the summer of 1939, a border dispute between Manchukuo and the Mongolian People's Republic led to the Battle of Khalkhin Gol, where Soviet and Mongolian forces defeated the Japanese Kwantung Army. On 8 August 1945 the Soviet Union declared war on Japan under the Yalta Conference agreement and invaded Manchukuo.

After the Battle of Leyte Gulf, the Japanese were unable to fight further surface engagements and resorted to kamikaze attacks. The Allies then used island hopping, invading Iwo Jima and Okinawa, which enabled a blockade of the Japanese home islands and the start of a strategic air raid campaign that caused widespread urban destruction. The war ended after the US atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August 1945.

Stalin secured from Roosevelt at the Yalta Conference in February 1945 a promise of territorial desires in the Far East. In return he agreed to enter the Pacific War within two or three months of Germany's defeat.

Between 2005 and 2010, a South Korean Truth and Reconciliation Commission investigated atrocities of the 20th century. It verified 4,934 execution victims of the Bodo League massacres of alleged communists by South Korean forces in 1950, though historians estimate at least 60,000 people were killed.

Japan had estimated that a Soviet attack was not likely in August 1945 or before spring 1946. Stavka had in fact planned a mid-August 1945 offensive and concealed the buildup of a force of 90 divisions, many of which crossed Siberia in their vehicles to avoid straining the rail link.

In 2010, a North Korean submarine torpedoed and sank the South Korean corvette ROKS Cheonan, killing 46 sailors. Later that year, North Korea fired artillery shells on Yeonpyeong island, killing two military personnel and two civilians.

literature.text: Until the 20th century, much of Korean poetry was written in Hanja. In the early 20th century there were attempts to introduce imagist and modern poetry methods, particularly through translations of early American moderns such as Ezra Pound and T. S. Eliot.

Poetry is quite popular in 21st century Korea, both in the number of works published and in lay writing. Lyrical poetry has dominated from the 1970s onwards. A corpus of modern Korean poetry is being compiled, providing linguistic information on 10,300 original Korean poems.

Japan's literature has gone from strong Chinese influence to wide international recognition. After the Meiji era's westernization, Japanese literature became more recognized abroad, leading to two Japanese Nobel laureates in literature, Yasunari Kawabata and Kenzaburō Ōe.

Jeong Ji-yong, born in 1902, has been described as "the first modern Korean poet." In 2007 the Korean Poets' Association listed him among the ten most important modern Korean poets. He translated English poetry and studied English literature at Japan's Doshisha University.

Jeong Ji-yong's poetry passed through three stages. Around 1925 to 1933 he wrote sensual imagist work that often focused on the sea. From 1933 to 1935 he composed religious poetry influenced by his Catholic faith, beginning with the poem Phoenix.

Natsume Sōseki's humorous novel I Am a Cat (1905) used a cat as its narrator. He also wrote the famous novels Botchan (1906) and Kokoro (1914). Along with Mori Ōgai and Shiga Naoya, he was instrumental in adopting and adapting Western literary conventions and techniques.

Avant-garde writers such as Kōbō Abe, author of The Woman in the Dunes (1960), wanted to express the Japanese experience in modern terms. They did so without using either international styles or traditional conventions, developing new inner visions.

After 1941's "Ongnyu Village" and "Guseong Village," Jeong Ji-yong's poetry showed the predominance of Eastern thinking in its aesthetic. In 1950, at the onset of the Korean War, the Government Preservation Department detained him, and he was then transferred to Pyongyang Prison. He is believed to have died there, around 1950; the article gives no cause or exact date.

Haruki Murakami is one of the most popular and controversial of Japan's authors today. His genre-defying, humorous and surreal works, including Norwegian Wood (1987) and The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle (1994–1995), have sparked debate over whether they are true literature or simple pop-fiction. Kenzaburō Ōe has been one of his harshest critics.

O Seyeong's volume Night-Sky Checkerboard was translated into English in 2016 and published in the United States. The Chicago Review of Books listed it as one of the twelve best poetry collections of 2016.

O Seyeong's early works contained significant amounts of "deconstructive" poetry, leading to his classification as a modernist poet. He gradually became fascinated with Eastern philosophies and used them to depict humanity's existential agony. His work draws on 'namelessness,' a Buddhist word for a state in which the mind is captured by desires and ego.

Donald Keene's 1988 book The Pleasures of Japanese Literature grew out of five lectures he gave between 1986 and 1987. Three were at the New York Public Library, one at the University of California, Los Angeles, and one at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It was written to introduce Western readers to Japanese literary qualities.

science.text: In 1926, Kenjiro Takayanagi demonstrated a cathode ray tube television with 40-line resolution. It was the first working example of a fully electronic television receiver. He had begun a research program on electronic television in 1924.

Japan's science and technology developed rapidly after the Second World War. High levels of support for research and development produced advances in automotive engines, television display technology, videogames and optical clocks. Japan is also considered a global leader in robotics, aerospace exploration and biomedical research.
In April 2008, Yi So-yeon became the first Korean to fly in space. She travelled aboard the Russian Soyuz TMA-12, part of South Korea's space partnership with Russia.

Japan developed the first HDTV systems in the 1960s, and MUSE/Hi-Vision was introduced in the 1970s. Digital broadcasting later replaced it: ISDB superseded both the NTSC-J analog system and the MUSE Hi-vision analog HDTV system.

Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) was founded in 2003 by merging three aerospace organisations. It developed the Japanese Experiment Module, KIBO, which was added to the International Space Station in 2007 and 2008. The HTV was used to transfer payloads to the station in 2009.

Since 1973, Japan has sought to depend less on imported fuel and more on nuclear energy. By 2008, with 55 nuclear reactors, it was the third largest nuclear power user in the world. The reactors provided 34.5% of its electricity.

South Korea has sent up 10 satellites since 1992, all using foreign rockets and overseas launch pads. Arirang-1 flew in 1999 and Arirang-2 in 2006. Arirang-1 was lost in space in 2008, after nine years in service.
In 1927 Kenjiro Takayanagi raised his electronic television resolution to 100 lines, which went unrivaled until 1931. In 1928 he became the first to transmit human faces in half-tones on television.

Digital terrestrial television using ISDB-T started in Japan in December 2003. Japan has adopted ISDB over other digital broadcasting standards. NTSC-J had served analog broadcasts from 1950 until the early 2010s.

Since 1990, twelve Japanese individuals have participated in space flights, two of them women. Two Japanese astronauts also served as commanders of the International Space Station, the last being Akihiko Hoshide.

Japanese color television started slowly because of high prices, and only 1,200 units were sold in the year color broadcasts began. As prices fell, sales grew from 4,000 units in 1962-1963 to 1.28 million in 1967 and over 6.4 million in 1970.

The Japan Science and Technology Agency runs J-STAGE, an electronic journal platform for science and technology information in Japan. It also operates Jxiv, a preprints server, and requires its grantees to follow an open access and open science policy.

politics.text: After the Japanese Emperor announced surrender by radio on 15 August 1945 and the Pacific War formally ended on 2 September 1945, the Allied occupation began, with United States commander Douglas MacArthur administering the country. In 1947 a new Japanese constitution was enacted, officially ending the Japanese Empire and forming modern Japan.

From 1910 to 1945, Korea was ruled by the Empire of Japan as a colony under the name Chōsen, the Japanese reading of Joseon. Japan had first made Korea a protectorate under the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905, and forced Emperor Gojong to abdicate in 1907.

At its apex, the Empire of Japan was one of the largest empires in history, counting mainland Japan, colonies, occupied territories and puppet states. The land under Japanese control reached 8,510,000 square kilometers in 1942, and by 1943 its occupied regions held 463 million people, more than 20% of the world's population. Its expansion was marked by aggression towards other nations, and the Japanese committed numerous atrocities and war crimes, killing millions.

The Imperial Japanese Armed Forces were dissolved during the Allied occupation and were later replaced by the Japan Self-Defense Forces in 1954. Reconstruction under the occupation continued until 1952, when the Treaty of San Francisco took effect as a peace treaty.

In 1931, Japan invaded Manchuria after the Mukden Incident, a staged event engineered by Japanese military personnel from the Kwantung Army as a pretext for invasion. The puppet state of Manchukuo was established the following year. The Chinese organized Anti-Japanese Volunteer Armies, and the pacification of Manchukuo required a war lasting several years. Japan then adopted a policy of founding and supporting puppet states in conquered regions, which became the basis for the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere from 1940.

Starting in 1944, Japan began conscripting Koreans into its armed forces. All Korean men were drafted to join the Imperial Japanese Army, as of April 1944, or to work in the military industrial sector, as of September 1944. About 200,000 Korean men were inducted into the army from 1944.

Korea remained part of the Empire of Japan for 35 years after annexation, from August 22, 1910, until August 15, 1945. Japan and South Korea both declared the 1905 and 1910 treaties "null and void" in 1965.

After the Allies defeated Japan in 1945, Tokyo's colonial control over its far-flung territories ended. The United States returned the Nanpō Islands to Japan in 1968 and the Ryūkyū Islands in 1972, while the Soviet Union occupied Karafuto Prefecture in 1945 and annexed it.

Under Japanese rule, virtually all industries in Korea were owned by Japan-based corporations or by Japanese corporations in Korea. As of 1942, indigenous capital was only 1.5 percent of total invested capital, and Korean entrepreneurs were charged interest rates 25 percent higher than Japanese ones.

Taking advantage of the Russian Civil War, the Imperial Japanese Army occupied northern Sakhalin between 1920 and 1925. Japan kept favorable coal and oil concessions there until 1944, and in 1943 Karafuto was elevated to naichi status.

A 1979 book by Rabbi Marvin Tokayer and Mary Swartz named the 'Fugu Plan' for 1930s memorandums, after the Japanese word for puffer-fish, a delicacy that can be fatally poisonous if incorrectly prepared. They allege it was first discussed in 1934 and solidified in 1938, but the 1940 Tripartite Pact prevented its full implementation.

philosophy.text: In pre-war Japan, German philosophy was eagerly studied and introduced. From the late Meiji to Taishō period, the Kyoto School tried to harmonize Western thought with Eastern thought such as Zen Buddhism.

Korean philosophy is described as practical, stressing self-cultivation, communal ethics and the integration of theory with everyday life. From the late 19th and 20th centuries, Western philosophical currents strongly influenced Korean academia and politics. After 1945, North Korea and South Korea took divergent paths.

Nishida Kitaro built an original philosophy by fusing Zen and Western thought, and it is called Nishida philosophy. He insisted on pure experience, in which there is no opposition between subjectivity and objectivity. His ontology derived from absolute nothingness.

Watsuji Tetsuro criticized Western selfish individualism. His ethics holds that human beings are not isolated but exist in relation to others. He is also well known for Climate and Culture, which studied the relationship between the natural environment and local lifestyle.

From 1948 to the early 1980s, South Korea was mostly influenced by a mixture of German idealism and Neo-Confucianism, under an authoritarian regime. After democratization in the late 1980s, philosophy there split among many Western schools, including Marxism, analytic philosophy, post-structuralism, liberalism and libertarianism.
Japan's Emphasis on political culture and national tradition rose as a reaction against westernization. This trend had an ideological side that legitimized imperialism and militarism or fascism.

Korean-American philosopher T. K. Seung was born near Chongju in 1930 and in 1947 escaped Chongju because of the influence of the People's Committee of North Korea, crossing the 38th parallel with a few friends. When the Korean War broke out in June 1950, he fled south to Busan ahead of the advancing North Korean army. After the war he studied at Yale, where he met existentialism and New Criticism, and later became a professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

Under the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, the Governor-General's Office recognized Shintoism, Buddhism and Christianity as religions. Confucianism's Chengkyunkwan was instead regarded as a school of economics and treated as a social education institution.

culture.text: In 1983, Nintendo released the Family Computer home video game console, which was localized in 1985 as the Nintendo Entertainment System in North America. Because it was reasonably affordable, people no longer needed a company's finances to buy a game system. Japan became the cultural exporter of the video game world.

Seollal, the Korean New Year, is believed to originate from the 3rd century, with evidence in a document titled Samguk yusa. During the Japanese colonization of Korea it was prohibited from being celebrated. It became an official holiday sometime between 1945 and 1950.

Japan's pet boom is traced to 2003, when cats and dogs combined, an estimated 19.2 million, outnumbered children under 16, at 17.9 million. By 2009 the figures were 23.2 million pets to 17 million children. The boom had a dark side: as households keeping dogs and cats increased during rapid economic growth, the number of dogs and cats euthanized at public health centers (hokenjo) run by local governments reached 1,221,000 in 1974. By 2023 it had fallen to only about 9,000, according to the Ministry of the Environment.

Around 60 to 70 percent of Japanese couples are wed in "nonreligious" Christian ceremonies, even though most Japanese people are traditionally Shinto or Buddhist. This makes Christian weddings the most influential aspect of Christianity in contemporary Japan.

South Korea banned Japanese pop culture after its liberation in 1945. After President Kim Dae-Jung visited Tokyo in 1998, the ban was lifted in three steps between October 1998 and June 2000. A fourth step, opening Japanese TV programs and popular music, was expected around the 2002 FIFA World Cup.

Korean shamanism, musok, survived systemic persecution throughout South Korea's political turmoil in the 20th century, and shamans were long oppressed and stigmatised. Under the 1962 Cultural Heritage Protection Act, several festivals and kut were preserved as intangible cultural heritage, and the mudang Kim Keum-hwa was designated a Living National Treasure in 1985. In the 1970s and 80s the pro-democracy Popular Culture Movement used shamanism as a form of protest against the government, painting shamans as bearers of Korean culture whose spirit-possession kut could give voice to those who had died for social justice causes.

The Japanese government was very suspicious of new religious movements and periodically tried to suppress them. Government suppression was especially severe from the 1930s until the early 1940s, when Japanese nationalism and State Shinto were closely linked. It tightened control over religious institutions seen as undermining State Shinto or nationalism and arrested members and leaders, including Onisaburo Deguchi of Oomoto and Tsunesaburō Makiguchi of Soka Kyoiku Gakkai, who were typically charged with violating lèse-majesté and the Peace Preservation Law.

Buddhist temples in South Korea rose from 2,306 in 1962 to 11,561 in 1997, while Protestant churches rose from 6,785 to 58,046. Buddhists grew from 2.6% of the population in 1962 to 22.8% in 2005. Between 2005 and 2015, Buddhism fell sharply to 15.5%.

Pink Lady took part in the World Song Festival in Seoul in 1980, becoming the first Japanese musicians to perform in a concert in Seoul. In 2023, imase became the first Japanese musician to enter the top one hundred of the Melon chart, reaching number 17.

Soka Gakkai has had a particular influence on Japanese politics since 1964, through its affiliated party Komeito. In 1999, an estimated 10 to 20 percent of the Japanese population belonged to a Shinshūkyō, or new religion.

A 2024 performance in Tokyo of Seiko Matsuda's 1980 song "Aoi Sangoshou", covered by the Korean band NewJeans, went viral in South Korea. It pushed the song up the Melon chart. Showa retro music has since gained popularity there, and MBN has broadcast the Korea-Japan Top Ten Show since May 2024.

Chirori was a dog who, instead of being put to sleep (euthanized), was discovered by a Japanese singer and trained to help the elderly. Her story is the basis of the 2004 film Walking With Dogs: Chirori and Tamaru, and there is now a statue in her honor. The Tokyo-based International Therapy Dog Association trains dogs with no owners into therapy dogs and sends them to nursing homes and hospitals across Japan.
